articles.title: Doggonit! City dog licensing hits an all-time low
articles.text:
Doggonit! City dog licensing hits an all-time low - WBEZ Chicago
Pippet sits at the Chicago Animal Care and Control center on the Lower West Side this summer. City Clerk Anna Valencia says the number of dogs with dog licenses is at an all-time low.
Nima Taradji for the Sun Times
City Hall
Politics
Money
Doggonit! City dog licensing hits an all-time low
City Clerk Anna Valencia acknowledged Friday that her office has issued just 4,100 dog licenses in a city with an estimated dog population of 635,000.
By
Fran Spielman
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Chicago’s bark has long been worse than its bite when it comes to cracking down on owners of unlicensed dogs, but there now appears to be no bite at all.
That much was obvious Friday when City Clerk Anna Valencia revealed during City Council budget hearings that her office has issued only 4,100 dog licenses this year in a city with an estimated dog population of more than 650,000.
That’s down from the already paltry 8,000 dog licenses last year, 18,000 in 2017 and 40,896 in 2013.
The cost of a city dog license is clearly not the impediment.
The license fee has been frozen for decades at $5 a year for spayed and neutered dogs, $50 for those that are not and $2.50 for dog owners who are senior citizens.
Valencia said the problem is ignorance. The city’s regulatory leash has been so loose for so long, most Chicago dog owners don’t even know that they’re required to buy city licenses for their dogs.
“People don’t know. And if you don’t have a marketing budget to tell people, they just don’t understand,” Valencia told the Sun-Times.
“There’s no marketing dollars. You can do as much free marketing as possible, which we have, but there’s 2.7 million people in this city. We’ve done some free PSA [public service announcement] stuff. That’s important, but it’s not gonna be enough to move the needle.”
Downtown Ald. Brendan Reilly (42nd) said the number of dog licenses issued by the city is “ridiculously low” because it has “never been a priority” for the city to enforce the legal requirement — even on the city’s own agencies.
Reilly said the city’s Commission on Animal Care and Control transfers roughly 10,000 dogs to adoption partners like PAWS and the Anti-Cruelty Society without issuing dog licenses before transferring the animals.
“The vast majority of dog owners want to comply with city laws, but many are unaware that the city even requires a license. The city should not be imposing licensing requirements without properly educating the public regarding their obligations,” Reilly told the Sun-Times.
“This has been an issue for decades and it appears compliance has dropped off even further. I asked the city clerk to make this a priority through a public education campaign that leverages free public service announcement air time on local TV and radio, as well as the city’s massive network of JCDecaux billboards, bus shelter ads and video kiosks.”
Ald. Ray Lopez (15th), the City Council’s resident dog lover, said the 4,100 dog licenses sold by the city — at a time when Cook County issues 500,000 annual rabies tags — shows that there is a “breakdown in communication that’s hurting the city’s ability to fully track” stray dogs.
“It’s not just about the revenue. It helps with identification and the return-to-owner law. If your pet escapes and has a valid city license tag on it, we’ll bring that pup home for free. It won’t go to Animal Care and Control because we’ll know where that dog belongs,” Lopez said.
“That’s the greatest value of the dog license. If one of my dogs were to escape, anyone could scan and see where that dog lives, bring him home and I don’t have to worry about him going to the pound.”
Currently, dog owners can obtain a dog license at the city clerk’s office or through the city’s clerk web site. But for years, dog owners who failed to purchase dog licenses have gotten a pass.
That changed in 2005, when the clerk’s office put computer software in place to match its short list of licensed dogs with Cook County’s larger list of Chicago dogs with rabies shots.
Warning letters were then mailed to those whose names appeared on the county’s list, but not the city’s, prompting a small boost in registration.
That’s the way it stayed until October 2011, when then-City Clerk Susana Mendoza’s outreach campaign and the threat of tickets prompted a larger surge in dog registrations.
On Friday, Lopez proposed requiring animal hospitals and veterinarians to purchase city dog licenses in advance like they do rabies tags, and issue them “at the point of vaccination.”
“Administer this tax as they would a sales tax in a retail environment,” Lopez said.
Valencia proposed a “universal dog license” that would be issued jointly by the city and the Chicago Park District.
“The Park District offers a dog license and we do. Instead of overlapping, we should do one together and split the cost. But we can’t do that until we get our new technology system,” she said.
Valencia made no apologies for letting dog licensing slide in favor of higher priorities: amnesty programs that give people debt relief; City Key IDs that help them get housing and enroll kids in school, and City Council modernization.
“We only have so many people and so many resources,” she said.

articles.title: Political groups spent $12 million to defeat CTU candidates. One losing race cost $76 per vote.
articles.text:
Political groups spent $12 million to defeat CTU candidates. One losing race cost $76 per vote. - WBEZ Chicago
Flyers paid for by political action committees and super PACs attacking Chicago School Board candidates that were sent to city voters during the fall campaign.
Justin Myers/Sun-Times
Education
Chicago School Board
Political groups spent $12 million to defeat CTU candidates. One losing race cost $76 per vote.
By contrast, the Chicago Teachers Union spent less than $8 per vote to help rack up wins in district races on Tuesday, a Sun-Times analysis found. The anti-CTU groups helped usher their preferred candidate for president to victory but spent big in several school board districts, only to lose.
By
Lauren FitzPatrick
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Political spending groups funded by an area billionaire seeking to defeat the Chicago Teachers Union in historic school board elections on Tuesday may have won their preferred president, thanks to their infusion of millions.
But in several school board district races, they spent their biggest money per vote — only for those candidates to lose, a Chicago Sun-Times analysis has found.
Common Ground Collective, which shelled out the most money by far through Nov. 2 — about $7 million — spent as much as $45 per vote to sway unsuccessful district races. Most of the cash spent by its political action committee and super PAC came from powerful billionaire Michael Sacks.
In District 1b on the Northwest Side, it spent $473,000 bolstering Michelle Pierre and attacking her opponent, who ultimately prevailed. That’s $43 per vote.
Similar trends held true for the cash-rich Illinois Network of Charter Schools, whose $4.4 million spending also funded costly defeats — as much as $31 a vote, according to an analysis of PAC and super PAC spending through Nov. 2 and vote totals available Nov. 5.
The big piles of cash that poured into the inaugural full board elections came mainly through independent super PACs that have no contribution or spending limits — and cannot coordinate with candidates. Through Nov. 2, spending aimed against CTU candidates by these two groups totaled $11.5 million. Another group consistently spending against CTU candidates,The Urban Center, bumps the total to $11.9 million.
The money aims to counteract the CTU’s built-in advantages — incumbency, an army of workers and established connections with some voters who are or were Chicago Public Schools parents.
But the money hardly guaranteed victory, and some candidates worry it backfired.
Pierre says the public confused the super PAC spending on her behalf with her own values — and voted as many Americans did Tuesday against candidates backed by the mega-wealthy.
“That definitely did not represent me,” the longtime educator says. “But that narrative was shared constantly. This narrative of billionaires intervening in elections probably had an impact.”
Both groups that sought to declaw the CTU did not manage to win a decisive majority. Though four races remain too close to call, CTU-backed candidates could win as many as 10 of 20 seats.
However, the two super PACs’ combined $4.6 million for Jessica Biggs for president appears to have paid off. They spent about $16 per vote, $13 of that from Common Ground, a new political group that aims to “defeat extremist efforts from both the far right and far left that seek to divide our city.”
Asked at a WBEZ campaign forum about the big money backing her, Biggs, who is a current board member, answered the question by leaning on her “voting record that shows my independence.”
Common Ground’s director Chuck Swirsky argues that come January, the union will be down from its current 15 members who were elected with CTU’s backing or appointed by ally Mayor Brandon Johnson, plus, their candidate for president, “Hilario Dominguez lost big — it’s a clear repudiation by the voters and the kids are worth it every time.”
The $16-per-vote to boost Biggs is a bargain compared to some district candidates who lost.
Spending on Peter Gonzales’ loss in near Northwest Side District 3a broke down to about $76 per vote.
Spending on Pierre’s loss in District 1b farther out on the Northwest Side broke down to about $71 per vote.
For Jesus Ayala Jr. in southwestern District 7a, each vote equaled $56 in outside spending. That race remains too close to call, with the CTU-endorsed candidate leading.
By contrast the CTU spent less than $4 per vote in these winning races. CTU PAC and Our Schools PAC, the two supporting union candidates, spent more than $2.6 million through Nov. 2, according to state board of elections filings. CTU has no super PAC.
Gonzales points to campaign finance law letting super PACs fund ads as long as they act separately from campaigns.
“That wasn’t anything to do with us, and we noticed this at the polls. People kept saying this, that we were somehow funded by Michael Sacks,” he says. “I’ve never met Michael Sacks … I didn’t take any money from Michael Sacks.”
Paralegal and CPS parent Connie Anderson in District 10b on the South Side fought her discouragement about disparate spending — about $50 per vote for her opponent versus less than $3 for her from CTU.
“Every day … another ad will come out, and another lie will come out, and you’re just like, ‘I don’t know what I got myself into,’” she said Tuesday night, declaring victory. “Then, lo and behold, you’re looking at the polls, and you’re like, ‘Wait, what? People believe in my platform.’”
The anti-CTU spending did pay off in a few key races, including the upset of incumbent Aaron “Jitu” Brown, an activist and catalyst behind the law that changed the board to an elected one.
It also helped keep retired school psychologist Therese Boyle in her Southwest Side District 9a board seat, with anti-CTU groups spending only $2 more per vote.

articles.title: The Rundown: Downtown ‘Cultural Stadium’ gains traction
articles.text:
The Rundown: Downtown ‘Cultural Stadium’ gains traction - WBEZ Chicago
Downtown Chicago on Oct. 1, 2026.
Victor Hilitski for the Chicago Sun-Times
The Rundown: WBEZ’s Daily Newsletter
The Rundown: Downtown ‘Cultural Stadium’ gains traction
Plus, why two school board races still haven’t been called. Here’s what you need to know today.
By
Bianca Cseke
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Good afternoon! It’s Friday — and my WBEZ colleague Sasha-Ann Simons’ last day as host of “In the Loop.” Here’s what’s next for the show. And here’s what else you need to know today.
1. A plan for a Downtown ‘Cultural Stadium’ is gaining steam with a new leader and $2 million funding
As my colleague Ambar Colón reports, former Michigan state Rep. Donna Lasinski was announced this week as the initiative’s inaugural president. Under Lasinski’s leadership, the Cultural Stadium plans to build on Chicago’s already vibrant arts scene and “transform existing infrastructure and underused public spaces into new cultural experiences,” according to a news release from the group.
Backed by $2 million in private, corporate and government funds, the idea for the so-called “Cultural Stadium” was created by Lou Raizin, president and CEO of Broadway In Chicago. The proposal aims to weave arts and culture into the everyday lives of Chicagoans, especially those working in or visiting the Loop.
Some programming has already emerged this year. Through a Cultural Umbrella pilot program that offered free days for children and their families to access the city’s major cultural institutions, more than 400 children and their parents attended events at places such as the Joffrey Ballet, the Chicago History Museum, Chicago Children’s Theatre and the Adler Planetarium. The effort was funded by a $50,000 grant from the Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events.
Also underway is “Poetry Way,” the creation of a digital display in the alley between Joffrey Tower and the Chicago Theatre in the Loop. The collaboration between the Poetry Foundation and the Joffrey Ballet launched during the Chicago Loop Alliance Arts Fest in October. A permanent debut is set for March 2027.
More Downtown alleys could be transformed under the Cultural Stadium. The website calls the project “Midblock” and aims to turn “overlooked alleys and service corridors” into vibrant and bustling gathering places. [ Chicago Sun-Times]
2. Missing Election Day results are holding up race calls in two Chicago School Board districts
Votes cast on Tuesday from almost every city precinct have been reported by the election board, including ballots from 44.6% of registered voters, or 686,000 Chicagoans. But as of yesterday evening, 12 of 1291 precincts had not been counted — down from 50 on Wednesday, WBEZ’s Cam Rodriguez writes.
The board counted an additional 12,000 votes Thursday, WBEZ’s analysis showed. There are 3,000 ballots from Election Day left to be counted, according to the board, and 131,131 uncounted votes in total, including mail-in ballots. More than 4,000 provisional ballots also remain to be tabulated.
When asked by WBEZ why delays in counting ballots from Election Day were occurring, a board spokesperson said there are “ongoing transmissions to our central data intake and tabulating system.”
This snafu means the outcomes of races for school board districts 5b and 7a are, for now, still too close to call. Two districts, 3b on the Near Northwest Side and 6a covering Downtown and the Near North Side, also haven’t been called, though all precincts have reported results. In both districts, fewer than 240 votes separate the top two vote-getters. [ WBEZ]
3. Illinois House Speaker Chris Welch says he will step down as caucus leader in the face of Democratic mutiny
Emanuel “Chris” Welch announced he won’t seek another term at the helm of his chamber next year, acknowledging his tenure was doomed after 26 Democratic state representatives signed a statement calling for a change in leadership, Mitchell Armentrout reports for the Chicago Sun-Times.
The seismic statehouse shakeup comes in the wake of revelations over the summer that Welch was aware of sexual harassment allegations against disgraced ex-state Rep. Harry Benton, D-Plainfield, almost three years before additional complaints prompted Benton’s resignation.
The call for new leadership was distributed late Wednesday by North Side state Rep. Kelly Cassidy, the most vocal public critic of Welch’s handling of the case and his formation of a working group that Cassidy dismissed as a “smokescreen” instead of addressing Springfield’s entrenched culture of harassment.
The statement demanding Welch’s ouster drew signatures from nearly a third of the caucus that will be sworn in with a new General Assembly in January, including Cicero state Rep. Lisa Hernandez, chair of the Democratic Party of Illinois.
“Over the course of the last few months, we have grown increasingly convinced that the House Democratic Caucus needs new leadership,” the lawmakers wrote. “We represent a broad spectrum of our caucus, and each has come to this decision for our own reasons. We look forward to a robust race for a new Speaker of the House.” [ Chicago Sun-Times]
4. An appellate court upheld the city’s decision to deny a Southeast Side metal-shredding business an operating permit over public health concerns
The relocated and rebranded General Iron scrap metal operation was built and ready to open at East 116th Street along the Calumet River in 2022 when then-Mayor Lori Lightfoot’s administration rejected the permit, citing the potential public health impact from air pollution. The business takes junked cars, large appliances and other sources to salvage and resell metal.

WBEZ announces three guest hosts for ‘In the Loop’
Mariah Woelfel, Araceli Gómez-Aldana and Susie An will bring their reporting expertise and fresh perspectives to the weekday morning show from November through January.
By
Anne Klingeberger

WBEZ today announced that three of its journalists will take turns guest hosting “In the Loop” over the next three months, bringing their reporting expertise and fresh perspectives on Chicago to the station’s weekday morning news and conversation program.
Mariah Woelfel, WBEZ’s City Hall reporter, will host in November, followed by engagement reporter Araceli Gómez-Aldana in December and “Curious City” editor Susie An in January. The rotation follows Sasha-Ann Simons’ final broadcast as host today as WBEZ conducts a search for the show’s next permanent host.
“We’re excited that three trusted voices from WBEZ will continue to bring listeners the news, culture and conversations they have come to expect from ‘In the Loop,’” said executive producer Dan Tucker. “We’re also deeply grateful to Sasha-Ann for the curiosity, warmth and thoughtful interviews she’s brought to the program for the last six years.”
Meet the Hosts
November – Mariah Woelfel, City Hall Reporter
Mariah covers the decisions made at Chicago City Hall and how they affect neighborhoods and everyday life. During her month behind the mic, she’ll bring her expertise in local government to conversations about the issues shaping Chicago, including interviews with candidates ahead of the February municipal election.
December – Araceli Gómez-Aldana, Engagement Reporter
Araceli’s reporting takes her into communities across Chicago, connecting with residents and exploring the issues that affect their lives. Her time as host will emphasize community perspectives and conversations about issues including affordability, technology and the changes shaping Chicago neighborhoods.
January – Susie An, Editor of “Curious City”
As editor of WBEZ’s “Curious City,” Susie helps uncover the stories behind Chicagoans’ questions about their city. She’ll bring that curiosity to “In the Loop,” exploring local history, neighborhood stories and the questions listeners have about how Chicago works.
“In the Loop” airs weekdays at 9 a.m. on WBEZ 91.5FM. Listeners can tune in live or find episodes at wbez.org or on the WBEZ app.

articles.title: In acclaimed 'Once Upon a Time in Harlem' documentary, a Chicago journalist emerges from obscurity
articles.text:
"Once Upon a Time in Harlem" documentary introduces audiences to Chicago journalist Gerri Major - WBEZ Chicago
Chicago-born journalist Gerri Major is a central figure in the new “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” documentary by William and David Greaves that is screening at the Black Harvest Film Festival in Chicago. She is pictured here in a portrait taken by Carl Van Vechten on March 22, 1935.

In acclaimed 'Once Upon a Time in Harlem' documentary, a Chicago journalist emerges from obscurity
William and David Greaves’ celebrated documentary introduces audiences to Gerri Major, a former editor at Ebony and Jet magazines. The film is one of the highlights of the Black Harvest Film Festival.
By
Erica Thompson

At the height of the Harlem Renaissance in the 1920s, the city bustled with activity.
People recited Langston Hughes’ “Weary Blues” poem on street corners. Duke Ellington delivered electrifying performances at the Cotton Club. A’Lelia Walker, daughter of millionaire Madam C. J. Walker, drew an enviable guest list to salons at her townhouse.
There to capture it all was Gerri Major, a glamorous journalist and Chicago native whose columns covered the Black upper class until her death at 90 years old in 1984. Nicknamed the “Harlem hostess,” she wrote for several newspapers before becoming a senior editor at Ebony and the society editor at Jet magazine.
Major is a central figure in “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” William and David Greaves’ critically acclaimed documentary playing in select Chicago theaters in November. The film, featured in the Black Harvest Film Festival running Nov. 6-15 at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago’s Gene Siskel Film Center, captures a party attended by Major, composer Eubie Blake, painter Aaron Douglas and more than 20 other Harlem Renaissance luminaries at Duke Ellington’s home in 1972.
In “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” Gerri Major describes herself as a “helpful” journalist to the Black community. “If I had a choice of saying something that would hurt our people or keeping quiet, I would keep quiet.”
Carl Van Vechten Papers/Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library
Major’s body of work is a detailed chronicle of Black life, history and genealogy, but she has remained an obscure figure — until now.
“She was an important journalist in terms of just raising the profile of what was happening with the people during that time,” said Liani Greaves, who is David’s daughter and one of the documentary’s producers. “The purpose of our film is to tell those stories to insert the renaissance into the cultural memory of the nation.”
Also a fashion icon, Major has a dress featured in the National Museum of African American History and Culture’s collection. She is a regal presence in “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” adorned in gold necklaces and bracelets and green rings that match her flower-patterned dress. In the documentary, she converses warmly with the other guests, including other Chicago natives: librarian Regina Andrews, historian Nathan Huggins and activist Louise Patterson.
Major also reminisces about throwing her own lavish parties at her home on West 139th Street, the cultural mecca known as “Strivers’ Row,” as well as her career.
She describes herself as a “helpful journalist” rather than a “great journalist.”
“If I had a choice of saying something that would hurt our people or keeping quiet, I would keep quiet,” she says in the film. “If I couldn’t do something that was going to give us a boost up, I was never going to give us a boost down.”
In 1953, Gerri Major joined the staff of magazines Ebony and Jet, covering major events such as the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II in England. She is pictured here in 1972 in a still from “Once Upon a Time in Harlem.”
Courtesy of Neon
Born Geraldyn Hodges in 1894, her exposure to Black socialites began in her childhood in the Douglas community area. She was given a debutante ball at 18 and earned a bachelor’s degree in philosophy at the University of Chicago. But her early life wasn’t without struggle, especially as one of few Black women at the college.
“We were humiliated and put down and crucified, but we stuck it out,” she says in the film.
Before moving to Harlem, she married Dr. Henry Binga Dismond, the first of her three husbands, and taught at Stephen A. Douglas Elementary School. She also participated on a commission to investigate the Chicago Race Riot of 1919.
Besides reporting for the New York Amsterdam News, Pittsburgh Courier and other outlets, she worked as a publicist, radio announcer and writer with New York’s public health department.
In 1953, she joined the staff of magazines Ebony and Jet, owned by the Chicago-based Johnson Publishing Company. She traveled frequently, covering the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II in England, writing about a dictator in the Dominican Republic and overseeing the company’s Paris bureau. Her column for Jet, “Gerri Major’s Society World,” ran until her death.
The critically acclaimed documentary “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” is showing at the Black Harvest Film Festival and in select Chicago theaters in November.
Courtesy of Neon
Together with Doris Evans Saunders, she wrote the 1976 book, “Black Society,” tracing the evolution of the Black upper class from the 1700s to contemporary times.
William Greaves initially sat on the “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” footage while continuing to shoot more content about the renaissance. After he died in 2014, his family worked to restore and release the film.
David Greaves, William’s son, said it was important to share the stories of Major and others in the documentary at a time when Black history is being removed from schools and other institutions.
Seeing the film is “an act of resistance,” he added.

Robyn Mineko Williams began her dance career with Hubbard Street Dance Chicago in 2000, fulfilling a childhood dream. “I saw Hubbard Street when I was 9 and decided, ‘That’s what I want to do, somehow,’” she said.
Her tenure with the company ended in 2012. Afterward, she started saying yes to more opportunities to make dances, transitioning her dream job toward choreographer-slash-performer. In 2014, she added mother to her list of roles.

“Traveling around doing choreographic commissions is really great, but it also can be a bit lonely,” said Williams, who is in her 40s.
In the hope of creating more on her own terms and therefore more at home with her son, she began a sequence of longer-development works that incorporate music, film and other media, with the help of aesthetically sympathetic friends. Her latest, “To Leave You,” premieres Nov. 9 and 10 at Three Top Lounge at the Salt Shed.
It’s difficult to summarize Williams’ role in the creation of “To Leave You” and its kin with a one-word job title such as “choreographer.” In assembling artists of several stripes and guiding their creativity with her prompts, she could be called a director, engineer or even a conductor. The finished pieces are grounded in dance, but the dance blurs into the music and visuals, and the pieces respond to the settings where they are performed.
“To Leave You” by Robyn Mineko Williams and ArtistsWhere: Three Top Lounge at the Salt Shed, 1357 N. Elston Ave.
When: Nov. 9 and 10
Info: threetoploungechicago.com
Making more than just dance and creating with others marks a distinct phase of her artistic career. “I think it’s the only way I’ve been able to evolve myself,” she said.
The tinder of “To Leave You” was Williams’ meditations on mortality. She considered what she would like to leave her now 11-year-old son, Knox, to remember, as if placing messages and memories in a box of keepsakes. For example, Williams’ grandmother taught her about knife technique, in a way that acknowledged their Japanese ancestry and showed a glimmer of individuality.
“She always told me to cut cucumbers on a diagonal,” Williams said, “and that’s [a memory] that would go in the box.”
Making more than just dance and creating with others marks a distinct phase of her artistic career. “I think it’s the only way I’ve been able to evolve myself,” Williams said.
Courtesy of Ricardo E. Adame
She assembled a group of artists she wanted to create with: the dancers Jessica Tong and Jason Hortin, her former companymates from Hubbard Street; the musician Nate Kinsella, of the band American Football; and Julia Miller, one of the founders of the puppet-forward performance collective Manual Cinema.
Through artist residencies at The Momentary in Bentonville, Arkansas, and at DESERTRADE in Twentynine Palms, California, the fivesome workshopped ideas for the piece, everyone bringing not only artistic skills but also personal histories, along with cherished mementos and family photographs. As the artists fueled the piece, it took shape and grew to encompass all of them in its world.
“Everyone is in the world together, and we’re all making this thing together,” Williams said. “So there wasn’t a separation between musician and visual artist and dancer. How do we do each of our things that we’re so well versed in, but find a seamless way to interact so you don’t feel that definition or line between the mediums?”
This loosening of the lines means everyone is participating in the dance in “To Leave You,” including Miller and Kinsella, whose performance lives do not normally involve dance.
“I will be moving around, or whatever you want to call it, in the piece,” Nate Kinsella said. Here, the bassist of American Football rehearses with Audrey Sides.
Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times
The tinder of “To Leave You” was Williams’ meditations on mortality. Here, Audrey Sides and Jason Hortin rehearse in the BalleX studios.
Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times
Miller said her training was at least dance-adjacent, coming from the more visual subgenres of theater. “Mostly theater that’s really physical,” she said, “like clown or commedia, and I brought that training into Manual Cinema.”
How her physical participation in “To Leave You” came about sounds like a case of being careful what you ask for. “I was like, ‘If you wanted me to move a little bit . . .,’” Miller said. “And then she put me in the show, which was really exciting and scary.”
Kinsella, too. “I will be moving around, or whatever you want to call it, in the piece,” Kinsella said. He worked previously with Williams on a music video for the song “Red Meadow” where he created the movements. “I guess it was technically dancing that I had put together for the two of us to do,” he said. She was impressed, and pointed to that experience when he initially balked at dancing in “To Leave You.”
“She said, ‘Actually, you are a dancer — you just don’t think of yourself that way,” he said.
